technology.heroTitle: Proof of capture that survives social media.
technology.heroSubtitle: C2PA attaches a camera signature to content data at capture. But that capture proof tolerates no modification to the content data whatsoever — and most social media platforms alter the data for display optimization. We needed a way to separate the capture proof from the content data itself, so that mathematical trust is preserved even after posting to social media.

issues.title: Why this matters
issues.intro: Across industries, the same crisis is unfolding: nobody can tell what's real anymore.

sns.label: Social media & creators
sns.text: Deepfake videos go viral with fabricated news logos. Creators face accusations that real content is AI-generated. Unauthorized reposting is the norm, and revenue goes to the copier, not the original creator.

media.label: News & journalism
media.text: Reporters face accusations that real footage was AI-generated. Video evidence, once considered conclusive, is now questioned by default. The speed of misinformation structurally outpaces correction.

insurance.label: Insurance & finance
insurance.text: An estimated 10% of insurance claims involve fraud. Damage photos, medical documents, and property listings can be fabricated with increasing sophistication. Recipients have no independent way to verify authenticity.

ai.label: AI, courts, healthcare, academia
ai.text: AI companies face billion-dollar lawsuits over training data rights. Forged documents challenge court evidence. Telemedicine images lack tamper verification. Research retractions rise as image fabrication becomes trivial.

c2pa.title: The right foundation already exists
c2pa.p1: The root cause of problems like deepfakes and unauthorized reposting is the same: the origin and rights ownership of digital content remain unknowable until actual harm occurs and someone makes a claim.
c2pa.p2: Technologies are being developed to enable verification of content authenticity and rights before harm occurs. There are broadly two approaches.
c2pa.p3: The first is post-hoc analysis — detecting fakes by examining content after creation, as with AI-based authenticity detection. But this is an arms race. As detection technology advances, generation technology that evades detection emerges. There is no structural advantage for detection.
c2pa.p4: The second is recording provenance with cryptographic signatures at the time of content creation. The security of these signatures depends on the integrity of signing keys, the certificate chain, and the correctness of the implementation. But unlike post-hoc detection, this approach has a structural foundation that is unaffected by advances in generation technology.
c2pa.p5: C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity), backed by over 6,000 organizations including Adobe, Microsoft, and Google, is the open standard for this provenance-recording approach. It records which device or software created the content, when, and what edits were made — all cryptographically signed.
c2pa.p6: Google Pixel signs photos with its Titan M2 chip. High-end Sony and Nikon cameras implement C2PA signing. OpenAI, Google, and Adobe sign their AI-generated content with C2PA. The infrastructure is real and growing.

gap.title: But proof disappears as content spreads
gap.p1: C2PA verification requires two things: the complete C2PA manifest data (a JUMBF container holding the signature chain, certificates, and edit history) and the complete data of the content itself. For a photo, that means the full-resolution capture data. For a video, the entire original video file. If even one byte of the content data changes, the hash will no longer match and verification fails. This tight coupling (referred to as hard binding in the C2PA specification) is an essential design for integrity guarantees, but becomes a barrier when content is distributed.
gap.p2: Nearly every social media platform, messaging app, and CDN strips the manifest and recompresses the content on upload. Facebook, Instagram, X, and YouTube all remove C2PA data and alter the content data for efficiency. Once that happens, verification becomes impossible. The World Privacy Forum calls this "the primary obstacle to C2PA interoperability."
gap.p3: Even when C2PA data remains in the file, cryptographically verifying the information inside it (camera capture proof, timestamps, edit history, etc.) requires both the complete C2PA manifest data and the complete content data. If either is missing, it is impossible for a third party to cryptographically confirm and retrieve that information.
gap.p4: Existing solutions include mechanisms like embedding URLs in watermarks and using cloud storage to recover C2PA manifests. But these are fundamentally approaches that attempt to approximately re-associate content data — which has already lost its cryptographic verifiability — with C2PA manifests.
gap.p5: To build a system where proof of camera capture actually reaches people on social media, we needed to solve a different problem: separating the proof — that the content had camera capture provenance recorded and passed C2PA verification — from the content itself, making it accessible in a trustworthy form even without the complete original file.

tp.title: Title Protocol: making proof independent
tp.subtitle: Extracting arbitrary attributes from content and recording them as standalone, independently trustworthy records.
tp.p1: Title Protocol takes C2PA-signed content and processes it inside a TEE (Trusted Execution Environment): hardware-isolated processing designed so that the server operator cannot access or alter the verification. While the cryptographic binding between the content and its manifest is still intact, it performs C2PA verification and attribute extraction, then seals the result with the TEE's own signature. This ensures the cryptographic chain of trust passes unbroken from the device's signing key to the TEE's attestation signature. The signed attributes are stored off-chain and linked to an NFT on the blockchain.
tp.p2: The result: provenance data that exists independently of the content. No original file needed. No trust in any specific company required. Trust is grounded in the TEE's hardware isolation, open-source verification code, and immutable records on the blockchain. Which device captured it, when, whether it was hardware-signed — these attributes can be queried through the blockchain.

step1.label: Sign at capture
step1.text: C2PA records the device information, date and time, and tools used, all sealed with a cryptographic signature.

step2.label: Verify in isolated hardware
step2.text: A TEE (currently using AWS Nitro Enclaves) verifies the C2PA data. The TEE is a hardware-isolated environment designed so that the operator cannot access the verification process. The verification result is signed with the TEE's internal key.

step3.label: Extract and record
step3.text: The verified attributes are extracted and linked to a compressed NFT on the Solana blockchain. Cost at current network conditions: ~$0.00015 per record. 100,000 records cost roughly $15.

step4.label: Anyone can verify, anywhere
step4.text: Your browser fetches data directly from blockchain nodes and verifies the TEE signature. No server is involved in verification, and no trust in any specific company is required. The proof exists independently of the content file.

stateless.label: Stateless TEE: two-phase processing
stateless.text: Verify: the TEE decrypts the content, verifies the C2PA signature chain, and returns the verification result to the client, signed with its own key and encrypted. Sign: after the client stores the signed result in any storage of their choice, the TEE confirms retrieval of that data and re-verifies its own signature, then constructs a blockchain transaction and partially signs it. The client applies the final wallet signature and broadcasts. This design means the TEE never needs to hold a wallet, never maintains state between requests, and can be restarted or replaced at any time. If a TEE instance is compromised, it holds no persistent keys or state, so the impact is limited to requests processed during that instance's lifetime. It cannot retroactively affect past records on the blockchain.

e2ee.label: Client-side encryption
e2ee.text: The content owner encrypts the content and wallet address on their own device before uploading. Encryption uses an ephemeral X25519 keypair: the client generates a one-time key, derives a shared secret with the TEE's public key (published on-chain in Global Config), and encrypts with AES-256-GCM. The TEE's response is also encrypted with the same derived key. Node operators see only ciphertext and cannot read, modify, or determine the destination wallet. The ephemeral key is discarded after use, providing forward secrecy.

coreExt.label: Core / Extension architecture
coreExt.text: Core records the C2PA provenance chain and rights structure. Extensions add computed attributes (perceptual hash, hardware signing proof, AI detection flags) as WASM modules executed inside the TEE. Extensions enable content lookup even after platforms strip the original metadata.

cost.label: Compressed NFT cost optimization
cost.text: Using Solana's Bubblegum compressed NFT standard, per-record cost is ~¥0.023 (~$0.00015) at current network conditions. 100,000 registrations cost roughly ¥2,250 (~$15).

security.label: Security considerations
security.text: TEEs are not infallible. Side-channel attacks have been demonstrated against some implementations (e.g., Foreshadow against SGX). Title Protocol mitigates this through multiple layers: (1) Stateless operation: no persistent keys or state survive across requests, so even if an instance is compromised, the impact is limited to processing during that instance's lifetime. (2) Wallet key separation: the TEE never holds the user's wallet key; it only partially signs transactions. (3) Client-side encryption: even if the TEE host is compromised, the node operator still cannot read content because encryption happens on the user's device. (4) Remote attestation: clients verify TEE integrity before submitting content. (5) All TEE enclave code is open source and independently auditable. The protocol also explicitly does not prevent provenance laundering (re-registering someone else's content). Similarity-based deduplication at registration time would destroy the low-cost design, so duplicate detection is handled at query time by applications. Content semantics (legality, appropriateness) are also outside protocol scope and are application-layer responsibilities.

comparison.title: What exists today and what remains unsolved
comparison.intro: C2PA verification services and provenance registries exist. Here is where the gaps remain.

scenario1.label: Proof that survives sharing
scenario1.text: C2PA data is stripped by nearly every platform. Existing solutions attempt to recover the full manifest via watermarks or centralized cloud. Title Protocol takes a different approach: verified attributes exist as independent records on the blockchain, so even after C2PA metadata is stripped from the file, the provenance data remains accessible without recovering the original manifest.

scenario2.label: Querying attributes without the file
scenario2.text: Existing services store full C2PA manifests externally, so you still need to parse the manifest to access specific attributes. Title Protocol extracts and records individual verified attributes, making them directly queryable from the blockchain.

scenario3.label: Cross-platform rights tracing
scenario3.text: When content goes viral, tracing the original creator requires searching across fragmented services, each with its own ID scheme. Title Protocol uses a content ID derived from the SHA-256 hash of the C2PA manifest signature. This is a value anyone can compute from the same C2PA content, independent of Title Protocol. Rights holders are linked by wallet address, enabling cross-platform tracing through a neutral, non-proprietary identifier.

scenario4.label: Trusting the verifier
scenario4.text: If a company runs the verification, you must trust that company. Title Protocol uses TEE: the verification is designed to happen in hardware-isolated processing where the operator cannot intervene. The result is cryptographically signed and client-verifiable. All TEE enclave code is open source, so the verification logic itself can be independently audited. The trust shifts from a company's reputation to a publicly auditable codebase and security model.

intro.title: How this verification works
intro.desc: RootLens verifies the provenance and authenticity of C2PA-signed content inside a TEE (Trusted Execution Environment — hardware-isolated processing that the server operator cannot access) and records the results on the Solana blockchain.
intro.trustChain: Trust is established through a chain of checks: the on-chain configuration defines trusted verification nodes → the NFT is confirmed to belong to the official collection → the off-chain verification data is fetched → the TEE signature is verified to confirm data integrity. Each step runs independently in this browser.

core.title: Core NFT — Provenance Record
core.desc: The Core NFT records the result of verifying the C2PA signature chain embedded in the content, signed by the TEE and stored on the blockchain. The entire provenance — who captured it, when, and with what tool — is preserved in a tamper-proof form.
core.collectionPass: This cNFT's Collection address matches the Core Collection address in GlobalConfig, and membership is verified. Confirmed as a legitimate cNFT issued by a trusted TEE node
core.collectionFail: This cNFT's Collection address does not match the Core Collection address in GlobalConfig
core.teeSigPass: Ed25519 signature over the serialized payload and attributes of the off-chain data verified against the TEE Public Key. Proves data has not been tampered with since TEE generation
core.teeSigFail: Ed25519 signature on the off-chain data could not be verified against the TEE Public Key
core.c2paFail: Could not confirm provenance chain record
core.offchainDesc: The TEE signs the verification result and returns it to the client, which stores it in off-chain storage. The TEE is stateless by design and never accesses storage directly.
core.noLinks: None (single content — no ingredient materials used)
core.creator: Registrant Wallet

ext.title: Extension NFTs — Attribute Verification
ext.desc: Extensions are objective attribute values computed by WASM modules inside the TEE from the raw content data. While Core handles the C2PA provenance chain (rights structure between content), Extensions handle properties of individual content (perceptual hash, hardware signing, etc.). There is no limit on the number of Extensions — new verification items can be freely added through new WASM modules.
ext.collectionPass: This cNFT's Collection address matches the Extension Collection address in GlobalConfig, and membership is verified. Confirmed as a legitimate Extension cNFT issued by a trusted TEE node
ext.collectionFail: This cNFT's Collection address does not match the Extension Collection address in GlobalConfig
ext.teeSigPass: Ed25519 signature over the serialized payload and attributes of the Extension off-chain data verified against the TEE Public Key
ext.teeSigFail: Ed25519 signature on the Extension off-chain data could not be verified against the TEE Public Key

pdq.title: image-pdq — Image Identity Verification
pdq.desc: PDQ (Perceptual hash by Meta) is a 256-bit numerical fingerprint of an image's visual appearance. A WASM module inside the TEE computes it from the original image and records it on-chain. The viewer's browser recomputes the PDQ hash from the displayed image using the identical WASM binary and Jarosz downsampling, then compares it with the on-chain value. If the Hamming distance (bit-level difference) is within the threshold, the images are deemed identical.
pdq.matchPass: Hamming distance: {distance} (threshold: {threshold} or less to pass)

hardware.title: {id} — Hardware Capture Proof
hardware.desc: This Extension cryptographically proves that the content was physically captured by the device's secure hardware (e.g., Google Pixel's Titan M2 chip or iOS Secure Enclave). A WASM module verifies the hardware signature within the C2PA signature chain, providing third-party verifiable proof of physical capture.

dyn.teeVerified: TEE ({teeType}) verified the C2PA signature chain and signed the result with Ed25519 key {pubkey}. The signed result is stored at {uri} and linked to NFT {assetId}.

why.title: Why You Can Trust This Verification
why.trustless: Why trustless verification is possible without the original C2PA data
why.trustlessDesc: The C2PA verification — validating the signature chain and hash-matching against the content body — was already completed inside the TEE. The TEE signed the verification result with its private key (Ed25519), and the client stored it in off-chain storage. Viewers only need to verify this TEE signature; there is no need to possess the original C2PA binary data. If the TEE signature is valid, it confirms that "a trusted execution environment certified that C2PA verification passed."
why.tsaDesc: An RFC 3161-compliant TSA (Time Stamping Authority) is a mechanism where a third-party authority cryptographically certifies the capture time. The TSA timestamp is embedded within the C2PA signature chain, and the TEE verified its validity before recording it. This ensures that no one — including RootLens — can falsify the capture time.
why.noServer: No RootLens server is involved in verification
why.noServerDesc: All data used in this verification is fetched directly from Solana RPC nodes and off-chain storage. The RootLens server serves the page and display images, but has no involvement in the verification process. You can confirm the network destinations in your browser's developer tools (Network tab).
why.oss: All source code is publicly available
why.ossDesc: All source code is published on GitHub. The verification logic on this page, the TEE code, and the underlying protocol — you can inspect everything yourself. Built on Title Protocol, an open protocol for content provenance.

check.c2pa_chain_pass: Provenance graph in C2PA signature chain: {nodes} node(s), {links} link(s). Records the edit history and material relationships from capture to present
check.c2pa_chain_fail: No provenance graph found in the C2PA signature chain
check.content_hash_match_pass: The query Content Hash matches the Content Hash in the off-chain data payload. Confirms the retrieved data is a record for this content
check.content_hash_match_fail: The query Content Hash does not match the Content Hash in the off-chain data payload
check.original_check_pass: Among all cNFTs with the same Content Hash, this cNFT has the earliest registration. Determined as the legitimate original via duplicate resolution
check.original_check_fail: An older cNFT with the same Content Hash exists. This content may be a re-registration
check.original_check_error: Failed to fetch data needed for duplicate resolution. Cannot determine if this is the original
check.wasm_hash_pass: The SHA-256 hash of the WASM binary (WASM Hash, computed by the TEE immediately before execution) matches an entry in GlobalConfig's trusted WASM module list. Confirms an unmodified, authorized module was used
check.wasm_hash_fail: The WASM Hash in the off-chain data does not appear in GlobalConfig's trusted WASM module list. An unknown or modified WASM module may have been used
check.wasm_hash_skip: GlobalConfig's trusted WASM module list is empty — comparison skipped (may be unset on devnet)
check.wasm_hash_missing: No WASM hash found in off-chain data. Extension NFT data is incomplete
check.pdq_identity_pass: Hamming distance between on-chain PDQ (256-bit perceptual hash computed by WASM inside TEE) and browser-recomputed PDQ (same WASM + Jarosz downsampling, from displayed image): {distance}. Pass: {threshold} or less (0 = identical, lower = more similar)
check.pdq_identity_fail: Hamming distance between on-chain PDQ (256-bit hash from TEE WASM) and browser-recomputed PDQ (from displayed image): {distance}. Exceeds threshold of {threshold} (0 = identical, higher = more different)
check.pdq_identity_skip: No PDQ data found in the Extension NFT
check.pdq_identity_error: Could not load the displayed image, so the browser-side PDQ recomputation was not possible ({reason})
check.hardware_signing_pass: Hardware secure element signature ({id}) detected in the C2PA signature chain. Proves physical capture by the device

overview.title: RootLens Documentation
overview.subtitle: How RootLens proves content is real — from camera sensor to browser verification.
overview.whatP1before: When you see a photo online, how do you know it's real? RootLens answers that question. It proves that a photo or video is
overview.whatP1after: — captured by a real camera, on a real device, without manipulation — and lets anyone verify that proof independently.
overview.whatP2a: Here is how it works at the highest level: a camera signs the content at capture time. That signed content is then sent — encrypted, end-to-end — to a
overview.whatP2b: , a piece of isolated hardware where nobody can see the raw content or tamper with the verification code. The TEE inspects the signature, extracts key facts (who signed it, what the image looks like), and signs the results with a private key that
overview.whatP2c: — not even the developers of this system. That TEE signature is the root of trust.
overview.whatP3chain: The results are then linked to on-chain records (cNFTs on Solana) so that anyone can find them. The actual verification data is stored off-chain, but it carries the TEE signature — so the blockchain is an index for discovery, not the container of the proof itself. A viewer's browser fetches the data via the on-chain pointer and re-verifies the TEE signature locally, without contacting any server.
overview.userP1before: A content creator publishes a photo through the RootLens app. This produces a shareable link (e.g.,
overview.userP1after: ). When someone opens that link in a browser, the page displays the photo along with a verification badge showing whether the proof checks out. Behind the scenes, the browser fetches the proof data via on-chain pointers and re-verifies the TEE signature locally — without contacting the RootLens server.
overview.termsIntro: Before going further, here are the terms you will encounter throughout this documentation:
overview.termC2pa: An open standard (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) for embedding provenance metadata into media files. When a camera signs a photo with C2PA, it creates a cryptographic proof of where the content came from.
overview.termTee: Trusted Execution Environment. Isolated hardware (a secure chip or enclave) where code runs and keys are stored such that nobody — not even the system operator — can access the internals.
overview.termCnft: Compressed NFT. A lightweight on-chain record on Solana. RootLens uses cNFTs as tamper-proof containers for verification results — not as collectibles or art. "Compressed" means they use Solana's state compression to keep costs low while remaining fully on-chain.
overview.termSignedJson: A JSON document containing a verification result, signed by a TEE's private key. Because the signature is unforgeable, the document is self-proving — it carries its own proof of authenticity regardless of where it is stored.
overview.termContentHash: A SHA-256 hash of the original content file. Used as the unique identifier that links the content to its on-chain proof.
overview.termPdq: A "visual fingerprint" of an image. Unlike a cryptographic hash (which changes completely if a single pixel changes), a perceptual hash stays similar across re-encoding, resizing, and minor edits. This lets the browser confirm that the displayed image matches the one that was originally verified.
overview.termGlobalConfig: An on-chain record on Solana that defines protocol-wide settings: which cNFT collections are official, which TEE nodes are trusted, and which verification code (WASM) hashes are approved. The browser reads this directly from the blockchain — never from a server.
overview.phasesIntro: The trust model has three stages.
overview.phase1proves: This content was captured by a specific device
overview.phase2proves: The C2PA chain was verified and the result was signed with a hardware-isolated key
overview.phase2trust: TEE hardware (the signing key cannot be extracted, even by system operators)
overview.phase3proves: The displayed content matches the TEE-signed proof
overview.phase3trust: Re-verifies Phase 2 proofs locally — does not require trusting RootLens or any server
overview.sourcesP1: RootLens is not limited to content captured by the RootLens app. It works with any C2PA-signed content: Google Pixel photos (signed by Google's Titan M2 chip), Sony and Leica cameras, and RootLens's own app-level signatures. All content types enter the same Phase 2 pipeline and produce the same kind of verifiable proof. The difference is only in Phase 1 — the trust basis of the original signature — and this difference is clearly displayed to the viewer (e.g., "Shot on Google Pixel" vs. "Shot on RootLens").
overview.phase1step1: Camera signs with C2PA at capture
overview.phase1question: Proves this device captured the content
overview.phase3question: Viewer re-verifies in their own browser
overview.bgTitle: Background: Why C2PA Alone Is Not Enough
overview.bgP1: C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) is an open standard that embeds a camera's cryptographic signature into content at capture time. Devices like Google Pixel, Sony, and Nikon cameras support it, and it is becoming the foundation for proving content provenance.
overview.bgP2: But C2PA has a structural limitation. Verification requires both the complete original content data and the manifest — if even one byte changes, the hash no longer matches and verification fails. Nearly every social media platform and messaging app strips C2PA data and recompresses content on upload, so the proof disappears the moment content is shared. Title Protocol solves this by separating the proof from the content and recording it in a form that can be verified without the original file.

trustModel.title: Trust Model
trustModel.subtitle: What you need to trust, what you don't, and why — honestly.
trustModel.mustTrustTitle: What You Must Trust. What You Don't.
trustModel.mustTrustP3: This is a genuine limitation, and we state it honestly. The roadmap is to transition GlobalConfig governance to a multisig and eventually a DAO, distributing this trust across multiple independent parties. But today, this is a centralized trust point.
trustModel.layerDeviceTeeWhy: The signing key cannot leave the chip
trustModel.layerDeviceTeeCompromised: C2PA forgery possible, but Platform Attestation must also be broken
trustModel.layerTpTeeWhy: Verification code and signing key are isolated in hardware
trustModel.layerTpTeeCompromised: Fake results possible, but WASM code is open source and its hash is on-chain — tampering is publicly detectable
trustModel.layerGlobalConfigWhy: Defines which TEEs, WASM hashes, and collections are valid
trustModel.layerGlobalConfigCompromised: Could register a malicious TEE or WASM. Mitigated by open-source auditability. Planned: multisig → DAO
trustModel.layerSolanaCompromised: Would mean all of Solana is compromised, not just RootLens
trustModel.layerRpcWhy: Reads blockchain data; a malicious provider could return fabricated state
trustModel.layerRpcCompromised: A single compromised RPC is a real threat. Mitigation: use a known-good provider, or query multiple independent RPCs
trustModel.layerStorageWhy: Self-proving — the TEE signature is verifiable by anyone
trustModel.layerStorageCompromised: Tampering detected by signature check. Downtime = unavailable, not forgeable
trustModel.layerIndexerWhy: Lookup caches; all results are re-verified on-chain and via perceptual hash
trustModel.layerIndexerCompromised: Can only deny service, not forge proofs (see below)
trustModel.serverIntro: A natural question: if RootLens has a server, what does it mean that verification doesn't require trusting it? The server does two things:
trustModel.serverConclusion: The server can cause a denial of service (you can't find the proof), but it cannot cause a false positive — both the cryptographic hash and the visual fingerprint would need to match simultaneously.
trustModel.attestationIntro: How do you know the Title Protocol TEE node is actually running inside genuine TEE hardware? Two layers of evidence:
trustModel.attestationConclusion: The first layer is sufficient for normal verification — if the cNFT is in the official collection, the TEE was trusted at mint time. The second layer provides a deeper, fully independent check that does not require trusting GlobalConfig at all.
trustModel.selfProvingP2: This means the storage provider does not need to be trusted. Regardless of where the data is stored, the browser can verify its integrity by checking the signature. If the data has been tampered with, the verification fails.
trustModel.globalConfigP1: GlobalConfig is an on-chain record on Solana that defines protocol-wide settings. The browser reads it directly from the blockchain — never from the RootLens server. It contains:
trustModel.globalConfigItem1: Which cNFT collections are official (prevents fake collections)
trustModel.globalConfigItem2: Which TEE nodes are trusted (their public keys)
trustModel.globalConfigItem3: Which verification code (WASM) hashes are approved (prevents tampered code)
trustModel.globalConfigP2: Because this data lives on-chain, the RootLens server cannot inject fake values. The browser reads the source of truth directly. However, whoever holds the GlobalConfig authority key can update these values — this is the governance trust point discussed above.
trustModel.honestText: Verification does not require trusting RootLens or any server — but it does require trusting TEE hardware. Governance is currently centralized (single authority key). The path to decentralization (multisig → DAO) is planned but not yet implemented. All verification code (both TEE-side WASM and client-side) is open source.

contentOrigins.title: How Content Is Signed
contentOrigins.subtitle: Two levels of content authenticity — hardware and app — and why RootLens treats them differently.
contentOrigins.hwP1: Some devices sign content directly at the sensor level using a dedicated secure chip. The private key is burned into silicon at the factory and never leaves the chip — not even the device's operating system can access it.
contentOrigins.hwPixel: Image came from this device's sensor, unmodified
contentOrigins.hwSony: Image came from this camera's sensor, unmodified
contentOrigins.appP1: RootLens provides C2PA signing for devices that lack hardware-level support. Instead of a factory-bound sensor-to-chip path, RootLens uses a combination of Platform Attestation and TEE key protection.
contentOrigins.appMechanisms: RootLens builds trust through three mechanisms:
contentOrigins.appAttestationP1: Before issuing a Device Certificate, the RootLens server verifies that the device is genuine and uncompromised:
contentOrigins.appTeeP1: The EC P-256 signing key is generated inside the device's TEE (Secure Enclave on iOS, StrongBox on Android). The private key never leaves the TEE — signing operations happen inside the chip.
contentOrigins.appPkiP1: The device's public key is certified through a three-layer certificate chain managed by RootLens:
contentOrigins.tradeoffText:
RootLens's app-level signing cannot match the sensor-direct guarantee of hardware signing. The camera-to-TEE path goes through the OS, so a sophisticated OS-level attack (virtual camera injection) is theoretically possible — though Platform Attestation rejects rooted devices and debug builds.

This trade-off is intentional. C2PA-capable hardware (Titan M2, Nikon Z9) is still rare. RootLens provides app-level authenticity proofs to bridge the gap until hardware signing becomes widespread. When it does, hardware-signed content can be published through RootLens with its stronger guarantee intact.
contentOrigins.compSensorApp: No — camera data passes through OS
contentOrigins.keyPointText: Phases 2 (TEE verification + cNFT minting) and 3 (browser verification) are identical for all content origins. The difference is only in Phase 1 — the trust basis of the original signature.
contentOrigins.prov2scenario: Hardware capture → edit on RootLens → publish
contentOrigins.prov2display: "Shot on Google Pixel, Edited on RootLens"
contentOrigins.provenanceP2: When you edit a photo in RootLens, the app takes the original file as an "ingredient" and creates a new C2PA manifest recording the edit. The original manufacturer's signature is preserved in the provenance graph, so the verification pipeline can trace the full history — from the original camera capture through each subsequent edit.
contentOrigins.hwTrustBasisText: The device manufacturer binds a signing key to the secure chip at the factory and signs the device certificate with their own Root CA. The entire path from sensor to signature is controlled by the manufacturer's hardware.
contentOrigins.hwRulesOutText: Virtual cameras, screen capture injection. The manufacturer's hardware architecture protects the signing key and attests that the signature was produced on that specific device. The exact boundary of hardware protection varies by manufacturer.
contentOrigins.appAttestationAndroidText: Key Attestation (proves the key was generated inside the TEE) + Play Integrity (proves the device is not rooted or running a debug build)
contentOrigins.appAttestationIosBefore: App Attest (proves the app is the genuine RootLens binary running on genuine Apple hardware), with
contentOrigins.appAttestationIosAfter: binding the attestation to the specific key
contentOrigins.appPkiLinkAfter: page for the full certificate profile and issuance flow.
contentOrigins.provenanceP1before: RootLens supports editing content after capture (crop, mask, trim). When content is edited, the C2PA standard handles this by creating a new manifest that references the original manifest as an "ingredient." This forms a
contentOrigins.provenanceP1after: — a chain of signatures that traces the content's full history from capture through each edit.

contentOrigins.appFlowNote2: Sensor-to-TEE path goes through the OS

titleProtocol.title: Title Protocol
titleProtocol.subtitle: An open protocol that extracts verifiable facts from content — without showing the content to anyone.
titleProtocol.whatP3: The TEE ensures the node operator never sees the raw content — only the extracted, signed facts leave the enclave. The trust comes from TEE hardware isolation: the signing key cannot be extracted, and the verification code (WASM) is pinned by an on-chain hash, so its correctness is publicly auditable.
titleProtocol.rlAppP1: RootLens is the first application built on Title Protocol. It uses the protocol to extract provenance information, certificate verification results, and perceptual hashes from camera content — then publishes the results as a shareable link. But Title Protocol itself is not limited to camera content or to RootLens.
titleProtocol.e2eIntro: No one — not the network, not the node operator, not RootLens — can see the raw content. Before sending content to a TEE node, the app establishes an end-to-end encrypted channel:
titleProtocol.e2eConclusion: The result is that the content travels encrypted at every stage. The TEE node operator, the network, and RootLens never see the raw content. Only the extracted facts leave the TEE — sealed with the TEE's signature.
titleProtocol.mintP1: After verification, the TEE mints cNFTs on Solana. Each content item produces:
titleProtocol.whatP1before: Title Protocol is a general-purpose protocol for extracting
titleProtocol.whatP1after: from C2PA-signed content. It processes content inside a TEE, seals the extracted results with a TEE signature, and links them to cNFTs on Solana.
titleProtocol.whatP2after: . The entire pipeline — from ingestion to result output — runs end-to-end encrypted. The TEE receives encrypted content, decrypts it internally, extracts the requested attributes, signs the results, and returns them encrypted. Only the extracted facts (e.g., "this certificate chain is valid," "the perceptual hash is X") are shared — never the content itself.
titleProtocol.agnosticP1before: The protocol does not care who signed the content. A Google Pixel photo and a RootLens photo enter the same pipeline. The difference is which
titleProtocol.agnosticP1after: processor verifies the certificate chain — the core extraction and signing logic is identical.
titleProtocol.processorIntroAfter: field — the name of the organization whose certificate signed the content (e.g., "Google" for a Pixel photo, "RootLens" for an app-signed photo). The app reads this field and tells the TEE which processors to run:
titleProtocol.processorCalloutB: processor verifies the C2PA certificate chain against
titleProtocol.processorCalloutBold: the corresponding manufacturer's Root CA public key
titleProtocol.processorCalloutC: , not RootLens's CA. When a Google Pixel photo is verified, the TEE checks the certificate chain against Google's Root CA — hardcoded inside a WASM binary whose hash is registered on-chain.
titleProtocol.producesP1before: For each processor, the TEE produces a
titleProtocol.producesP1after: — a JSON object containing the verification result, signed with the TEE's private key (currently Ed25519; the protocol is designed to migrate to post-quantum algorithms as they mature):
titleProtocol.producesP2c: . JCS (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) ensures that the JSON is serialized in exactly one way — otherwise, logically identical data could produce different bytes and break the signature. The signature is trustworthy because the private key is locked inside TEE hardware (it cannot be extracted), and the TEE will only sign data produced by the approved verification code (whose hash is pinned on-chain). Both the key isolation and the code integrity are necessary for the guarantee.

titleProtocol.wasmP2before: When a browser verifies a cNFT, it checks that the
titleProtocol.wasmP2after: in the payload matches a hash registered on-chain. This ensures the TEE ran a known, unmodified verification binary — not one with a backdoor or weakened Root CA.

cnftStructure.title: cNFT Structure
cnftStructure.subtitle: All cNFTs share the same base structure. The processor type determines their role.
cnftStructure.coreP1: The Core cNFT records the C2PA provenance graph — the chain of signatures showing who created the content and how it was modified.
cnftStructure.payloadIntro: The payload contained in the signed_json pointed to by the cNFT's URI. Protected by TEE signature.
cnftStructure.coreContentHash: SHA-256 of the active manifest signature
cnftStructure.coreNodes: Provenance graph nodes. Each has {id, type} where type is "final" or "ingredient"
cnftStructure.coreLinks: Relationships between nodes. Each has {source, target, role} (e.g., "audio", "image")
cnftStructure.coreTsa: RFC 3161 timestamp (Unix seconds), only if C2PA TSA exists
cnftStructure.coreTsaPubkey: SHA-256 hash of TSA certificate (only if TSA exists)
cnftStructure.coreTsaToken: Base64-encoded RFC 3161 token (only if TSA exists)
cnftStructure.checkTeeSigText: Hardware-isolated key signature (currently Ed25519) over JCS-canonicalized payload
cnftStructure.checkProvenanceText: At least one node exists in the C2PA graph
cnftStructure.checkOriginalityText: Earliest Core cNFT for this content_hash
cnftStructure.extP1: All Extension cNFTs share the same base structure, with WASM execution results flattened into the payload.
cnftStructure.extPayloadIntro: In addition to common fields, WASM output is merged into the payload as the result.
cnftStructure.extContentHash: Same content_hash as the Core cNFT
cnftStructure.extWasmHash: SHA-256 of the WASM binary (verifiable against GlobalConfig)
cnftStructure.extInputHash: SHA-256 of extension inputs (only if WASM uses auxiliary inputs)
cnftStructure.extResultDesc: WASM execution results are flattened into the payload. The output fields are deterministic per processor and documented in each cNFT section below.
cnftStructure.certP1: Records the result of verifying the C2PA certificate chain against the corresponding manufacturer's Root CA. The extension_id indicates which Root CA was used:
cnftStructure.certGoogle: Verified against Google's Root CA public key
cnftStructure.certSony: Verified against Sony's Root CA public key
cnftStructure.certLeica: Verified against Leica's Root CA public key
cnftStructure.certRootlens: Verified against RootLens's Root CA public key
cnftStructure.certResultDesc: The WASM output contains: verified (boolean result), certs_der (array of Base64-encoded DER certificates), root_ca (name of the Root CA used), and root_spki (hex-encoded Root CA public key info).
cnftStructure.pdqP1: A 256-bit perceptual hash computed using the PDQ algorithm (Meta ThreatExchange compatible). A visual fingerprint that survives re-encoding and minor resizing.
cnftStructure.pdqResultDesc: WASM output: pdqhash (64-char hex), quality (integer 0-100, gradient energy metric), algorithm ("pdq"), bits (256).
cnftStructure.pdqHowP1: PDQ is a 256-bit perceptual hash algorithm developed by Meta (formerly Facebook) for the ThreatExchange project. The algorithm works as follows: the input image is converted to grayscale using BT.601 coefficients, smoothed with a Jarosz filter (box×2 = tent), and downsampled to 64×64. A 2D DCT (Discrete Cosine Transform) is applied to extract the top-left 16×16 low-frequency coefficients (256 values, excluding DC). The Torben algorithm computes the median, and each coefficient is quantized to 1 if above the median, 0 otherwise, producing a 256-bit hash. Re-encoding and minor resizing produce similar hashes; substantially different images produce substantially different ones.
cnftStructure.pdqVerifyP1before: The browser recomputes the PDQ hash from the displayed image using a pure TypeScript implementation, then compares using
cnftStructure.pdqVerifyP1after: (the number of bit positions where the two hashes differ). The threshold of 31 (out of 256 bits) follows Meta ThreatExchange's recommended similarity threshold.
cnftStructure.vpdqP1: Computes PDQ hashes per keyframe (I-frame). Two filters apply: only frames with quality ≥ 50 (gradient energy metric) are included, and near-duplicate frames (Hamming distance ≤ 10 from the previous frame) are pruned.
cnftStructure.vpdqResultDesc: WASM output: frames array (each with pdqhash, quality, keyframe index), frame_count (number of output frames), algorithm ("vpdq-keyframe").
cnftStructure.vpdqVerifyP1: The browser extracts keyframes via WebCodecs + mp4box.js, recomputes PDQ, and matches. The current client implementation requires ≥ 80% of on-chain keyframes to match within the Hamming distance threshold (a client-side heuristic, not a protocol-defined parameter).
cnftStructure.overviewP1: All cNFTs share the same fundamental structure. The only difference is their protocol role (Core or Extension) and which processor ran inside the TEE. Each content item produces one Core cNFT and multiple Extension cNFTs.
cnftStructure.onchainP1: The cNFT metadata on Solana follows the Metaplex Bubblegum standard. Only minimal identification is stored on-chain — the actual verification data lives in the off-chain signed_json.
cnftStructure.onchainUri: URI pointing to the signed_json (off-chain storage)
cnftStructure.onchainCollection: Core or Extension collection (defined in GlobalConfig)
cnftStructure.onchainP2: All data needed for verification (content_hash, provenance graph, WASM output, etc.) is in the signed_json at the URI, protected by the TEE signature.

verification.title: Client-Side Verification
verification.subtitle: Every verification check runs in the viewer's browser. The server provides an initial content lookup but is not involved in any trust-bearing verification step.
verification.flowTitle: What Happens When You Open a Link
verification.commonIntro: Every cNFT — Core and Extension alike — goes through the same three common checks:
verification.check1P1: The cNFT's collection address must match the official collection defined in the on-chain GlobalConfig. The browser fetches GlobalConfig directly from Solana RPC — never from the RootLens server, never hardcoded.
verification.check2P2: This is the most critical check. The TEE signature is what makes the proof unforgeable — the private key exists only inside TEE hardware and cannot be extracted by anyone. The browser re-verifies this signature entirely via the Web Crypto API, with no external service involved.
verification.check4P1: The C2PA provenance graph must contain at least one node. An empty graph means no provenance information was recorded.
verification.check8P1: The browser recomputes the PDQ hash from the displayed image using a pure TypeScript implementation. The Hamming distance to the on-chain hash must be ≤ 31 out of 256 bits (Meta ThreatExchange's recommended similarity threshold).
verification.check8P2: This proves the image you are looking at is the same image that was verified by the TEE — independent of any server.
verification.check9P1: The browser extracts keyframes via WebCodecs + mp4box.js, computes PDQ for each, and compares against on-chain hashes. The current client implementation requires ≥ 80% of keyframes to match within the threshold (a client-side heuristic, not a protocol-defined parameter).

pki.title: PKI Architecture
pki.subtitle: RootLens's three-layer certificate hierarchy for app-level content signing.
pki.shortLivedP1: Device Certificates are valid for only 90 days. This limits the window of exposure if a device is compromised. Certificates are renewed automatically 14 days before expiry in the background, without blocking the user.
pki.kmsTitle: KMS for Root and Intermediate CAs
pki.kmsP1: The Root CA and Intermediate CA private keys live inside AWS KMS and cannot be exported.
pki.bindingIntro: The server must verify that the public key in the CSR matches the key attested by the platform:
pki.androidKeyAttest: The attestation certificate chain's leaf certificate contains the public key that was generated in the TEE. The server compares this public key with the CSR's public key. A match proves the CSR key lives in the TEE.
pki.rotationP1: The app periodically checks whether the stored Device Certificate was signed by the current Intermediate CA. If the ICA has been rotated (e.g., due to a security incident), the check fails and the app re-provisions a new Device Certificate.
pki.scopeTextBefore: This page describes the PKI used for
pki.scopeTextAfter: . Hardware-level signers (Google, Sony, Leica) use their own PKI managed by the respective manufacturer.
pki.isolationP1before: iOS and Android have separate Intermediate CAs, each with its own KMS key. If one platform's ICA is compromised, it can be revoked without affecting the other platform. The
pki.isolationP1after: on each ICA prevents further delegation.
